bundleName: data publication the old ways part 1.json

name: Name
body:
"I want a scary story tonight."
The young prince was finishing his evening ablutions as Katya turned down his bed. "You will have nightmares," she told him matter-of-factly.
The young prince spoke in unaccented Khadoran—speech and enunciation were among the lessons he received each day—while Katya’s Umbreyan accent was still strong. It was partly why she had been chosen as one of the prince’s many governesses, tutors, and valets. Not the accent itself, but where it was from. Her connection to old Umbrey and a part of the prince that was now lost.
"I hardly ever have nightmares," Vlad said as he came from the washbasin and sat on the edge of his bed.
"Oh really? Then what do you dream about?"
The prince thought about this for a moment. "Warjacks, lately. I wish that I could be a warcaster, like my father was."
"Be careful what you wish for, little prince," Katya said, smiling. "A warcaster carries a heavy burden."
He lay down in his bed, and she tucked the blankets up around his shoulders. Here in the palace, it was not so cold, even in the midst of the Khadoran winter, but still there was enough of a chill that the blankets were welcome.

name: Name
body:
"Very well," she said, "a scary story, if I can manage one. I will tell you a tale that my mother told me. A story about the old lands, the old ways…"
***
In a small village near where my mother grew up, there was an old woman. A widow whose children had all preceded her into Urcaen, she had no family left to care for her, and so she lived a poor, simple life in a small shack on the edge of town. She earned her bread by washing laundry, but she was also a midwife, when the need arose, and knew how to make a poultice that drew out venom or fever, which leaves could be chewed to relieve an ache or a cough.
In those days, the word "witch" was still a dangerous accusation, but no one in the little village thought of the woman that way, even when she was seen talking to the trees at the edge of town or leaving offerings of food in the woods. They simply said that she kept to the "old ways."
At the other end of town, a farmer lived in the largest and finest house in the village. He had inherited the land from his father, who everyone in town said had been a good man until the tragedy. The father had two sons, and his wife died bringing the younger of the two into the world.

name: Name
body:
The older son had been a good man, like his father, devout and generous, a good steward of the land. But he had died on a hunting trip with his younger brother. They said he fell off a high cliff and broke like a doll on the rocks below. The father wept openly when his son’s body was laid to rest in the family plot, and he was never the same again.
It didn’t take long for father to follow son, and then the younger brother inherited everything. He had always been a cruel and ungrateful child, or so the people of the village said, and his good fortune made him worse rather than better. He became a miser who spent money freely only on drink. When he tried to hire someone from the village to work his land or in his big house, he invariably accused them, sooner or later, or trying to cheat him, and before long no one would come to work for him.
The farm gradually fell into disrepair. The house became dark and cluttered, the fences went unmended, the fields overgrown. Then, the farmer’s sheep began to go missing, and his suspicious eyes were cast upon the other members of the community, even as everyone knew that wolves or other wild beasts were likely making off with those animals that didn’t simply wander away through the broken fences.

name: Name
body:
As the farmer began to make threats and accusations, the people of the town held a meeting to discuss what to do. The farmer was not invited, yet he arrived anyway, reeking of uiske and slurring his words, a gun in his hand with the firing pin primed.
"I know what you’ve been doing," he shouted as he pushed his way into the town’s small meeting hall, sweeping the barrel of that gun around to point at first one person and then another. "Stealing my sheep. Lurking around my property. You think I haven’t seen you out there in the dark? Trying to scare me? Leaving those marks on my door? I know you all hate me. Think you can scare me away skulking in the woods. But it’s not going to work. I see you out there, and I’ll kill the next man who sets foot on my property, mark my words."
It was then that the old woman stood up.
"It’s the woods," she said, pointing a finger at the farmer. "They know what you did. And they won’t leave you be until you’ve made amends."
"You shut your mouth, old crone," the farmer said, training his gun on her.

name: Name
body:
"Your father knew the old ways and kept to them," the woman said. "The forest knew him, just as it knows you, and it will take what is owed."
"You shut your mouth!" the farmer shouted, and this time his pistol added a shout of its own. The shot caught the old woman in the chest and she fell. The farmer looked with horror at the gun in his hand, then dropped it and ran out into the night.
Now, at last, the townsfolk had something they understood. The cruelty and suspicion of the farmer were one thing, but now he had committed murder, and the men of the town gathered torches and weapons and marched to his farm.
What they found there was not what they expected. The front door of the farmhouse had been torn from its hinges, great gouges carved into the woodwork. Of the farmer himself, there was no sign, and he was never seen again. And that was the end of it, save for one man, who swore that he heard the farmer’s voice screaming and crying and praying out in the dark, and when he followed the sound while the other men searched the house, thought he saw a shadow, shaggy and antlered and dark, like a part of the night itself come to life, carrying the screaming farmer into the woods.

name: Name
body:
***
By the time Katya had finished her story, the young prince was breathing evenly, and she blew out the candle beside his bed and withdrew into the adjoining parlor, leaving the door to his bedchamber slightly ajar, the way he liked it. There were gaslights throughout the palace and a fire in the hearth, but she kept a candle close beside her as well, for she found the small flame comforting. No sooner had she seated herself with some needlepoint she had set aside earlier in the day, however, than the candle suddenly flickered and guttered, and she felt the prick of the needle against her finger, a jewel of blood shining.
Something was wrong. The feeling was as inescapable as it was inexplicable, and there was no hesitation as she took up the candle and strode toward the young prince’s room. The rooms were closed up, yet she felt an icy draft as she approached the partially open door, heard the soft beating of bird’s wings in the room beyond. Had the young prince opened a window?
But no, he was still in his bed, still sleeping peacefully. Yet he was not alone. It was there, on the other side of the bed, in the shadows. Hunched and wrong-shaped, it crouched over the prince like a nightmare, all tatters and furs and claws of ragged iron that reached out toward the sleeping shape and grasped the child even as Katya screamed, the candle in her hand going out and plunging the room into darkness.

name: Name
body: The dream is so familiar by now that, even within its confines, she can recognize it as such. The small cabin filled with golden light from an afternoon sun. The distant sound of birdsong, presaging Khadoran spring. The faint scent of chamomile flowers that fills the air. And, most of all, the two children who sit on the floor before the dying hearth, dark of hair and dark of eye. She knows them both, even as she knows that she has never seen either of them before—nowhere, that is, except in the dream. One plays with a wooden toy carved in the shape of a warjack while the other arranges blocks painted with letters that, for some reason, she cannot read. They rise as she approaches and look at her expectantly. What are their names? *** Sorscha Kratikoff awakened as the bottle of cheap vyatka slipped from her fingers. Despite her state, she caught it with her other hand before it struck the warped floorboard of the small outpost. Some things die hard; the muscle memory developed as a warcaster was one of them.

name: Name
body:
She had dozed off slumped over the wooden table in her quarters, and every part of her ached, especially her head, a persistent throbbing that she chased with another swig of the vyatka. The pain also helped to drive away the memory of the dream, however, and that she welcomed.
Through the room’s one grimy window, she could see that the sun was already high in the sky, meaning she had missed whatever passed for reveille among the outcast soldiers under her command in this distant and half-forgotten corner of the kingdom. It wasn’t the first time, and it wouldn’t be the last.
Standing and stretching until she felt her vertebrae rearrange with a satisfying series of pops and cracks, she pushed the door open and stepped out into a wall of frigid air that blasted the wind from her lungs and sobered her up more than she might have preferred.
This far north, it would probably have been cold even if it hadn’t been the dead of winter. Gravewater Lake was to their south, and the nearest rail line was Skirov, more than five days’ march away. Sometimes, she was told, the snow here stayed in the shady places, even through the summer. Now it lay three inches thick, even in direct sunlight, and crunched beneath her feet as she stepped out of the cabin, her breath steaming in the air.

name: Name
body: When she was dispatched here by her superiors, she was told that it was an important strategic point due to its proximity to the Rhulic border. That was a lie, though. She knew it, and so did they. Rhul had always been Khador’s most peaceable neighbor and the only one upon which the empire had no immediate designs. The only fighting this area had seen in decades was during the Claiming, when the former Great Princess Regna Gravnoy of Hellspass had revealed her allegiance to dark powers and plunged that isolated city into a horror from which it never recovered. That had been years ago now, and even if there were still infernal monstrosities prowling what was left of Hellspass, it, too, was several days of hard marching away from the middle of nowhere outpost where Sorscha found herself consigned. Buried, more like, she thought, taking another swig of the vyatka. To her left was the barracks, little more than a long log cabin where twenty soldiers of the Winter Korps ostensibly under her command slept in shifts, drank, and played cards.

name: Name
body:
Pathetic excuses for troops—not one of them would have lasted a day nearer to Korsk or at any less peaceful time in Khador’s history. About half of their number were old enough to have previously been members of the Winter Guard, since disbanded and reformed by order of the empress. The other half were one more transgression away from a court martial, sent to this nameless outpost as a final stopgap before being drummed out of the service entirely.
Beyond the barracks was the unheated shack that served as workshop and storage for the one warjack they had sent with her as a fob toward the pretense that she was still an active warcaster: an ancient and beaten-to-hell Kodiak that probably should have been decommissioned years ago.
When she was younger, Sorscha had resisted naming her ’jacks, sticking with the teachings of the Druzhina that said they should only be referred to by number so that warcasters did not get too attached. Like so many other things, however, that was a relic of a time when she had lost less and cared more. Now she simply called this one Bear.

name: Name
body:
A soldier stepped outside to piss against the wall of the barracks only to stop and hastily button his breeches back up when he saw her standing in the snow.
"Kommander Kratikoff," he said, saluting awkwardly, "we didn’t expect you to be awake so early."
Sorscha looked up at the sky, judging from the position of the sun that it was nearer to noon than to dawn.
"Has anyone gone on patrol yet?" she asked the young soldier, whose name she thought was Vasilov or Vasily or something like that.
"They probably should," she continued, without waiting for an answer. "Just to keep up appearances."
Realizing he was dismissed, Vasily or Vasilov stumbled back through the snow and into the barracks to relay the order—or what passed for one.
When Sorscha stepped back into her quarters, she realized immediately that something was wrong. Frostfang leaned against the wall near her bed. She estimated it would take her three paces to reach it, a powerful mechanika weapon she had been allowed to keep, even in her unofficial exile, probably because it had been designed especially for her; no one else, in her experience, had ever managed its unusual balance successfully in battle.

name: Name
body:
She could reach it in a breath and, if she needed extra time, a spell had come unbidden to her mind, the cold of it numbing her fingertips, one that would slow any enemy for the necessary seconds she might need to be ready for combat. Old habits did, indeed, die hard, it would seem.
Despite the unshakeable sensation that something was off, however, there was no one in her cramped quarters. The only thing that had changed since she left was that the single window was now open, letting in a draft of cold air, and on its sill was perched a black crow that looked at her expectantly, its head cocked to one side. One of its eyes was beady and black; the other was scarred over and milky but not, she somehow knew, blind.
"No," Sorscha said to the bird. "I know what you want, but I’m not going to follow you. I’m going to sit down at this table, I’m going to finish the rest of this bottle, and then I’m going over to the barracks and see if I can confiscate another one."
The crow let out a loud, raucous caw, and Sorscha cursed under her breath.

name: Name
body:
Sorscha was not surprised to find the crone waiting for her in the clearing a quarter-mile from the outpost. The crow had led her there unerringly, stopping every few paces to look back expectantly and wait for her to catch up as she trudged through the snow, swearing periodically.
The figure could easily have been mistaken for a pile of rags and furs were it not for the iron claws that clutched a long, gnarled staff covered in writhing faces. Sorscha knew the Old Witch of Khador, the woman—if woman, indeed, she was—known as Zevanna Agha. She had fought beside her and her strange scrapjack, now nowhere to be seen, in battles that felt like a lifetime ago.
Sorscha also knew the stories that surrounded the ancient crone. The ones that said she had been there when Menoth first set foot on Caen, waiting to meet him, just as she now waited to meet Sorscha in this unadorned clearing. Though she knew that the Old Witch had the Motherland always at heart, Sorscha had never trusted the crone and trusted her less now than she had in the past.

name: Name
body:
When she thought of the Old Witch, Sorscha inevitably thought of Vlad. The so-called Dark Prince had always had a strange relationship with the old woman. "She was like a grandmother to me, even when I was a boy," he had said, and Sorscha knew that it was only the intervention of the Old Witch that had delivered Vlad from death’s doorstep—or maybe beyond it—when he fell in the Thornwood.
Yet as far as Sorscha could tell, it was the machinations of the witch that had led her lover to sacrifice himself twice over, first for the sake of the Motherland and then, more permanently, for all of Immoren as he died at the battle of Henge Hold, trying to throw back the tide of the infernals. He had died a hero, just as he had lived, yet Sorscha didn’t want a dead hero. She wanted a live man, the only one who had ever made her feel like a woman instead of just a soldier.
"You have a cold heart," he had told her once, as they lay together wrapped only in furs and one another. "A frozen heart is an asset on the battlefield. It can make terrible choices. Make the kinds of strategic sacrifices that a warrior has to make. But there is one thing it can never do: truly sacrifice itself."

name: Name
body:
Even then, he had talked of sacrifices. For the Motherland, for the war, for a history and a world of which Sorscha was no part, despite her military titles or her status as a warcaster. Vlad had been all that was left of a kind of ancient nobility, something she, as the daughter of a common soldier, felt she could never understand. And, ultimately, it had taken him from her, first into the arms of the empress herself and then into the even more unforgiving arms of death.
"You are looking vell," the witch said by way of greeting, a lie as obvious to her as it was to Sorscha herself.
Sorscha spat in the snow, an act that would have been terrifying to her when she was younger when she still felt she had anything left to lose. "What do you want?" she asked. "I’m not one of your playthings."
"You are a daughter of Khador," the Old Witch replied.
"I am the daughter of a dead man. There is not much else left."
"Perhaps more zen you think," the witch said, and Sorscha was surprised and frustrated to hear a note of sympathy in her crackling voice. "The vorld has asked much of you, Sorscha Kratikoff. It has taken much from you. But today it needs you again, and you vill rise to ze occasion."

name: Name
body:
"Find another puppet," Sorscha said, beginning to turn away. "I am done with your schemes."
"Zen ze boy vill die," the Old Witch said and, despite herself, Sorscha arrested her motion. "And ze line of Tzepesci dies vith him and, vith it, perhaps all Khador itself vill fall."
Slowly, as though she were an insect being trapped in amber—and perhaps to the Old Witch of Khador, that’s exactly what she was—Sorscha turned back. "Tzepesci?"
"Come here, child," Zevanna Agha said, and from behind a tree, on the edge of the clearing, a boy stepped forward. Sorscha had never been good with children, even when she was one, but he couldn’t have been more than ten years old. What was more, she recognized him instantly. Dark of hair, dark of eye, the boy in her dream, playing with the toy warjack.
"You know whose child zis is?" the Old Witch asked, and suddenly Sorscha did. Before her stood the offspring of Vladimir Tzepesci and the empress herself, the crown prince of all Khador.
"What are you doing?" Sorscha asked, hating how breathless she sounded. "What have you done? They will be after him. The Winter Korps. All of Khador itself will be on your shadow."

name: Name
body:
"Zey have bigger vorries now," Zevanna Agha said. "As do ve all."
"What are you talking about?" Sorscha asked. She was still hungover, though the cold air had done much to chase the remnants of the night’s drinking away, and now she cursed the fuzziness inside her own head. She had expected something absurd, frustrating, infuriating when she followed the crow to meet the Old Witch. She had never expected this. "We’ve been at peace for years."
"Zer has never been peace in Khador," the Old Witch said sadly. "Merely vaiting. Now, ze vaiting is over. You know ze prophecy, even if you do not belief it. You must take ze child vhere he vill be safe. In Old Korska, you vill find new allies, ze ones ve vill need if Khador is to survive."
"Why me?" Sorscha demanded, her head still spinning. "And what allies could I possibly find that could defend him better than the entire might of the imperial capital?"
"I have cast ze bones, seen ze omens in ze clouds," the witch said, gesturing with one of her iron claws at the heavens above. "If Khador is to survive, zis is how it must be."

name: Name
body:
For a moment, Sorscha stood swaying, the import of everything that she was being told crashing over her. The boy waited in silence, looking up at her with those dark, familiar eyes, and that very familiarity was the splash of cold water that she needed to shake her from her daze. The dreams, the prophecies, they made it all feel very unavoidable, but she was through being a plaything of fate. Cold iron ran down her spine, something she hadn’t felt since the last time she had commanded a warjack in battle.
"Then take him there yourself, since you can apparently just jaunt here and there as you please," she said. The anger behind the words felt good, melting a bit of the ice in which she had been slowly encasing herself for months now, maybe even years.
"If Khador is to survive," the Old Witch said again, "zis is how it must be."
Sorscha shook her head. "And if I told you that I no longer care much whether or not Khador survives?"
The Old Witch moved. It was a gesture impossibly fast, especially for one so ancient and stooped and gnarled as she. Sorscha’s instincts were honed to a razor’s edge, and even her current dissolute state had done little to dull them, and yet she was not fast enough to defend herself as one of the witch’s claws darted out and touched her cheek, ever so gently, just enough to draw a tiny line of blood.

name: Name
body:
The effect was similar to when Sorscha put her mind into one of her warjacks. She was still aware of her body, standing in the snow, her limbs hanging limp at her sides, but she was also aware of so much more. She saw great black ships on the horizon, coming in by the dozens. Ships she did not recognize and yet knew all too well—knew from stories and nightmares.
She saw armies of men and beasts, and she struggled to tell where one ended and the other began. She saw cities in flames—Skrovenberg, Ohk, Port Vladovar. She saw noncombatants cut down in oceans of blood, and worse, she saw those who were not slain but taken, shackled and bound to wait for a more hideous fate in smoking pyres and grisly ceremonies of sacrifice to terrible things from beyond.
When the vision had passed, Sorscha dropped to her knees in the snow. "The Orgoth," she said, barely able to force the name through numbed lips.
"Our old enemy has returned," Zevanna Agha said. "And Khador vill be but ze first to fall."
***

name: Name
body:
The child stumbled along behind Sorscha in the snow, and she had to stop every few dozens paces to angrily wait for him to catch up. His name, she knew, was Vlad, but she couldn’t call him that, couldn’t think of him as that. In her mind, he was just "the child," and when she spoke to him, her words clipped and harsh, she called him "kid."
The third time she stopped to wait for him he looked up at her and tripped over something buried beneath the snow, falling to his hands and knees. She expected him to start bawling, and she was already clenching her fist against the coming waterworks, but instead he simply stood, his mouth set in a firm scowl, and brushed the snow from the miniature greatcoat that was wrapped around him.
Every other time, she had started walking again before he drew abreast of her, but this time she waited a beat longer so that he could fall into step beside her.
"Is this your first time away from the palace?" she asked, her curiosity overpowering her desire not to be drawn into conversation.

name: Name
body:
He shook his head. "I’ve been outside the city walls a few times. We took a boat trip on Lake Volningrad once. But I’ve never been far from the capital before."
"You don’t seem very worried about it."
"I was," he admitted, wiping his damp sleeve ineffectually against his nose. "But then the old lady told me that she was bringing me to you. You’re famous! There are pictures of you in the palace. Katya—that’s my governess—she told me that you’re a national hero. And they say . . . they say that you were my father’s friend. Were you good friends?"
She thought of Vlad’s arms around her, his chest beneath her palms. "I hope so. I hope I was a good friend."
"I never knew him," the boy said softly. "I hear about him all the time. He was a great man. A hero, like you. But that’s not like knowing him."
"No," Sorscha agreed. "It isn’t." For the first time since she had followed the crow into the clearing, she felt a twinge of empathy for the kid. They both missed the same person, even if he had no idea who that person was.

name: Name
body:
"The old lady said that your father was a soldier," he said when she didn’t contribute anything else.
"The old lady says a lot of things," she replied and then chewed over her next words for several steps. "My father was a soldier. Not so lucky as me."
"Did he want you to become a soldier?"
For a moment, Sorscha’s eyes squeezed closed, and she was thirteen years old again, tears in her eyes, begging her father to take her with him as he walked out the front door of their little house. "Don’t worry, Sorscha," he had said. "I’ll be home again soon." It was a promise he couldn’t keep.
The rest wasn’t memory but imagination, fueled by the stories she had heard of the Boarsgate Massacre. A little Khadoran village on the Ordic border had decided to secede. They had taken a liking to the Ordic troops stationed close to them at Boarsgate. Unfortunately for them, the soldiers who were sent to investigate were led by Orsus Zoktavir.
He may not yet have earned the nickname the Butcher of Khardov, but he was already a subject of superstitious fear. Over seven feet tall and as strong as a warjack, Zoktavir was one of the most powerful—and one of the most fanatical—warcasters to serve the empire. And when he heard that the people of that little village were turncoats, something red and vicious broke loose inside him.

name: Name
body:
The story went that he killed every single person in the place. Men, women, children, until the mud of the streets had been turned to bloody soup. And when his own soldiers tried to stop his slaughter, he killed them, too. Including a Winter Guardsman by the name of Luka Kratikoff—Sorscha’s father.
Zoktavir had been brought before the empress—then still just Queen Ayn—in chains, under the heaviest guard of any prisoner to ever be tried in the palace. Rather than condemn him for his crimes, however, she had pardoned him, praised him.
"This prisoner is more loyal than any man here," she had said, and the Boarsgate Massacre had become a symbol of the price for disloyalty to the Motherland. Good, honest, simple soldiers like Sorscha’s father became pieces of propaganda.
Worse still, when Sorscha followed her father’s footsteps into the Winter Guard and was elevated to warcaster due to her innate sorcerous talents and her ability to control the huge, metal monsters that were so integral to warfare in the Iron Kingdoms, she had been forced to serve alongside Orsus Zoktavir. To fight beside the beast who had butchered her father. To match her troops with his, to use her own strategy to support his attacks. At times, to sacrifice those under her command—simple Winter Guardsmen, like her father had been—to safeguard his life.

name: Name
body:
And she had done it. She had hardened her heart, as she had learned to do from a young age. Frozen it, as Vlad had said. She had fought by the Butcher’s side when the need arose, but she had never stopped hating him.
Now, out here on the ragged edges of the world, having lost everything that she thought she was fighting for, she realized that she had let her heart thaw a bit, and that thawed heart was an open, aching wound in her chest.
When the Old Witch had shown her the coming of the Orgoth, she had seen something else. Perhaps the devious crone had meant for her to see it, perhaps not, but she had seen it nonetheless. A familiar monster, riding at the head of the enemy forces. The Butcher of Khardov, now transformed into something else, something even more horrible than he had been before, his hand encased in an iron gauntlet, shackled to a massive axe that screamed with the twisted faces of a thousand slain souls.
That was what was coming—and Sorscha was going to be there to meet it.

name: Name
body:
Orsus Zoktavir had heard dozens of stories about himself over the years. His was the name that the enemies of Khador whispered with only slightly more terror than his own troops. They said that he was a demon from the abyss, that he was raised in a cave by wild bears. They said that his mother had been an ogrun and his father a Kossite woodsman. That he was the last of a clan of Devourer-worshipping cannibals from deep in the forests of the north. That he was the personification of the Motherland herself, there to punish Her wayward children. That he had simply been another man who loved a girl until she died, and he went mad.
He no longer knew which of the stories were true, if he ever had.
Mad, though, he certainly had been. For years. Maybe forever. He could no longer tell the difference between memory and hallucination, but whichever it was, he could picture in his mind’s eye the empress of Khador, a woman he had sworn to serve and protect with his life, clamping the fell axe around his hand, condemning him to torment and wandering. Punishing him horribly—more horribly still than he was willing to remember now.

name: Name
body: And for a long time, the axe had tormented him. From the shrieking faces on its massive surface came the voices of all those he had slain, and they were so many. Hundreds. Thousands. The voices of enemies but also of friends and comrades. Women, children, his own soldiers. When he fought, sometimes a madness descended over him, and when that happened, it didn’t matter from where the blood flowed, so long as it came bright and hot and red. The voices tormented him no longer, though. Oh, he could still hear them. All of them. Thousands of them. Like a great choir. But now they told him a simple truth: that this is who and what he had always been. Whatever the realities of his origins, he had spent his entire life trying to solve a puzzle box. The puzzle of violence. The puzzle of how he fit into the world. He had thought he found the answer when he swore his oath to the empress, but he had been wrong. To her, he had only been a weapon. Useful while it lasted but easily cast aside when its purpose was fulfilled.

name: Name
body: Now, though, he had found something else. The place where he fit. The place where he had always belonged. It had been the axe that brought him here. For longer than he could possibly name, he had roamed the wilderness like an animal, killing whatever he came across, sometimes eating his prey raw, simply to give himself the strength to move on to the next kill. Then there were the ships with their black hulls and red sails. He didn’t really remember seeing them. To him, they had just been more targets, and the axe had dragged him to them until he was standing on the beach and gradually sinking into a quagmire of blood as bodies grew in piles around him. That was when she had come. Her voice pierced through those shrieking from the axe. It told him who he was, what he was, and for the first time in longer than he could say, he was calm. Only then did he realize the identity of those he had been slaying. They were nothing that he had seen before. Nothing that anyone in all of western Immoren had seen in centuries. Yet they were a story that everyone knew. The ancient enemy. The Orgoth had returned.

name: Name
body:
The woman who approached him in that mire of blood and gore was one of them. On her back were wicked blades; in her hands, curved swords. The armor she wore was similar to the warcaster armor that he had once claimed, though the light that glowed from it was an unfamiliar amber.
In the past, he would have dropped to his knees before her, and he knew from her bearing, from her demeanor, that she would have expected him to. But he did not. Instead, he simply let the axe drift to the bloody ground, its hilt still clamped inexorably in his hand. She nodded at him. He had come home.
***
Sorscha kicked open the door of the barracks, which hit the bunk behind it with a satisfying crack. Fifteen of the twenty soldiers under her command were in the barracks. Six played cards around a table in their shirtsleeves, two of them smoking thick cigars. One was carving near the iron stove that provided both warmth and a surface for cooking, while the others lounged or dozed in their bunks. Directly across from Sorscha, a soldier with unlikely red hair snored loudly, one leg dangling from her bunk, seemingly unperturbed by the sudden intrusion.

name: Name
body:
One of the soldiers at the table stood up and dropped his cards to scatter on the floor, swinging his arm into an ungainly salute. His face was angular, his chin pointed but softened by a beard flecked with gun-metal grey, and the bars on his coat—which was hung over the back of his chair—showed him to be a sergeant, the only officer in the place besides Sorscha herself.
"K-kommander Kratikoff," he said. "We weren’t expecting you." It was an excuse that never would have flown back when she was actually a real soldier, truly in charge of anything. Even as he said it, the others were only gradually rising to attention, while the red-headed soldier continued to snore.
"We have new orders," Sorscha said, suppressing the smile that threatened to betray her amusement at the discomfiture of the soldiers. "How soon will the patrol be back?"
She knew full well that the "patrol" was likely out in the woods somewhere drinking cheap vyatka and looking at dirty pictures.
"They aren’t expected for some time," the sergeant said, covering well. She thought his name was Agrinov. "I’ll dispatch Sergei—I mean, Private Mikolovich to bring them back."

name: Name
body:
"How did we get new orders?" the carving soldier, who had still not risen to attention, asked. "No one has been here in weeks."
"Oh, I’m sorry," Sorscha said, taking a further step into the room. "I was not aware that your promotion had come in and that you were a kommandant now. How lax of me not to realize that you outranked me. Please, my ignorance is unforgiveable. You must take me outside and make an example of me."
At the edge of ice in her voice, the carving soldier dropped his knife to clatter on the floor and rose to attention, his arm snapping up to his bald pate in a sharp salute. "My mistake, Kommander Kratikoff."
Now Sorscha did allow herself to smile, although it was the grin of a hunting cat. It had been a long time since she felt much of anything and, for the moment, it felt good.
"You have thirty minutes to have everyone assembled, Sergeant Agrinov," she said, hoping she was right about his name. "And fire up Bear. I expect us to be ready to march within the hour."
"March," the sergeant stammered, once again forgetting his military decorum, which he had set aside for so long here in the middle of nowhere. "But . . . where are we going?"

name: Name
body:
Sorscha had already begun to turn and head back out the door, bound for her own cabin and the suit of warcaster armor that hung there, unworn for months.
"South," was her only reply.
***

name: Name
body: The child had waited in the snow while Sorscha spoke to the troops, and now he followed her into her cabin, standing awkwardly next to the pot-bellied stove, snow melting off his boots and puddling at his feet as she got her warcaster armor down from its pegs on the wall and laid it out on the table. "You want to know about your father, kid?" she asked, as she undid the buckles on the warcaster armor. "Come over here and help me get this on, and I’ll tell you something about him. Something no one else would ever dare to tell you." Nodding eagerly, the child hurried over and began worrying at the buckles of the armor. Sorscha’s warcaster armor was lighter than most, designed to accommodate her unique combat style by providing her with optimal mobility. Over the years, she had gotten pretty good at putting it on herself and even stoking the furnace without much help. But she figured the kid should work, not just watch. "Blood is nothing," she said. "You’ve probably been told your whole life about how you’re the last of the Tzepesci line. The son of a hero and the empress herself. But none of that matters. Your father was a great man, it’s true. But he was great because of what he did, who he was, not because of how he was born. And however you turn out—great or disappointing—will be because of what you do, not because of who your father was."

name: Name
body:
She looked at the kid to see how he was taking this, but his head was down, his eyes on the buckles. "Out there, it doesn’t matter who your father is. The trees don’t care. The snow doesn’t care. And if the enemy cares, it is only ever to your detriment. None of those soldiers out there needs to know who you are, do you understand? From now until we get where you’re going, your name is Tobias, and you are no one’s son. Your only parents at the Motherland. Is that understood?"
The child looked up at her, and she found herself momentarily shaken by the glance of those dark eyes, so much like her dream. She struggled to read his expression, but he set his mouth in a firm line and nodded. "I understand."
***
To his credit, Sergeant Agrinov had everyone assembled in the snow by the time Sorscha got her warcaster armor on and stepped out to inspect them. The soldiers who had been out on patrol were back, and even Bear was down from its harness in the shack, its coal furnace sending up puffs of steam in the chill air.

name: Name
body: The red-haired, snoring soldier turned out to be Gridya, the closest thing they had to a mechanik and the only one in the group who could ’jack marshal in a pinch. She was standing next to Bear, huddled close to take advantage of the heat put out by the warjack’s boiler. Now that Gridya was awake, Sorscha recognized her face and vaguely remembered drinking with her a few times, though she generally preferred to drink alone. From one end of the loose line to the other, the soldiers looked like what they were: individuals who had been drummed out of every other posting available and sent to the ass-end of nowhere to be forgotten. Their coats were threadbare, patched, or still had obvious holes. A couple had lost their coats entirely and wore furs. One had two coats on, having won the second in a card game, or so he said. Their boots were scuffed and worn and, in at least one case, were not regulation boots at all. Despite all that, they stood in a line in the snow and waited for her at something resembling attention, even if some occasionally shuffled their feet or rubbed their arms against the cold. Sorscha marched from one end of the line to the other, and as she passed, they straightened, held their heads up higher. They were not used to receiving anything like leadership from her, but months of lax command had not entirely diminished her legend in their eyes.

name: Name
body: "As I’m sure you’ve all already heard," she said, "we have new orders. This is Tobias," she gestured toward the kid, who had been trailing along behind her, attempting to match her march. "He may not look like much, but Tobias is a strategic asset to the Motherland. And what does that mean?" She didn’t let the question hang long in the cold air—no reason to torture them. "It means that any one of you will step in front of a bullet that was meant for him, just as you would for me. Is that clear?" A ragged chorus of assent from the troops. "Our new mission is to escort Tobias south to Old Korska. That should be a relatively easy march, through friendly territory, and we’re going to expect to make good time accordingly. But we are also going to treat this as though an ambush could be lurking anywhere along the route, and so we are going to keep our guard up and have advance scouts at all times. Is that clear?" One of the soldiers awkwardly raised his hand. Sorscha had to resist the urge to laugh aloud at this schoolboy mannerism.

name: Name
body:
"Yes, soldier," she said.
"What’s in Old Korska?" he asked timidly.
"Unfortunately," Sorscha replied, "that information is given out on a need-to-know basis only. And, as of this moment, not even I apparently need to know."
***
Once upon a time, the great Cathedral Ohkskaya had been a wonder of the Motherland. Built of the white stone for which the White City of Ohk got its name, the Cathedral had housed more than a thousand sculptures depicting important figures and pivotal moments from the history of Morrowan faith. At one time, Orsus Zoktavir had walked through its halls before, though he could no longer remember why. Not an especially religious man—at least, not where Morrow or Menoth were concerned, his faith tied to other things that were personal to him and not easily communicated—he had nonetheless felt the power and the hush of the massive building.
Now whatever holiness it had once held was long gone, along with most of the statues, which were either broken or simply missing from their vestibules. The white stone was stained with smoke and, in many places, the rusty brown of dried blood.

name: Name
body:
Once the gathering place of Khadoran nobility, the White City had fallen to the Orgoth invaders, despite walls forty feet high and a dozen thick. The scars of the battle were everywhere in the city beyond the Cathedral, and they were inside as well. Defenders of the faith had held out as long as they could, and the marks of the gradual withdrawal deeper and deeper into the structure could be seen in scarred stone and torn tapestry.
Now, in a blasphemous inversion, it was one of the gathering places of the Orgoth command. To enter its great doors, Orsus had passed pits dug for the sacrifice of slaves to the Felgoeth, to whom his new comrades owed their power and longevity—their very souls. Did he owe his soul as well? The voices in the axe said so. He was not so sure.
It was to this structure that he had been called by a messenger from Sabbreth, the Eternal Annihilation. She was the one who had found him on that beach, and since then, she had been his connection to the Orgoth, his commander among the forces he now served.

name: Name
body:
He had been outside the city walls when the messenger arrived; he seldom spent much time within them, if he could help it. He was more comfortable on the field of battle or, if that was unavailable, on the edges of the wilderness.
His command tent was set up near the bank of the Wolveswood, where the flat expanses around the city itself gave way to the first fringes of the trackless Scarsfell Forest to the north. That was where he had been planning out their next strike, his keen tactical mind undimmed by his years, perhaps decades, spent lost in madness.
Nonetheless, a summons from Sabbreth was not to be ignored, and so he had come. The room to which he was led had once been the main chapel of the Cathedral. It was massive, the ceilings vaulted to the heavens, the light pouring in through stained glass windows. Unlike the rest of the Cathedral, this chamber was largely untouched by the Orgoth, though the pews had been smashed to kindling and removed wholesale to make room for troops, should any need to be assembled.

name: Name
body:
What had once been a place of worship was now a throne room, and in the place of power stood not Sabbreth herself but a new figure, one Orsus had never seen before. At a glance, she looked similar to Sabbreth, but there were differences even to Orsus’s untrained eye. Her armor was not that of a warcaster but more closely resembled what he had seen the Orgoth warwitches wearing.
Blades sprouted from the back of this new figure in even greater profusion than from Sabbreth’s armor, and as Orsus approached, he saw that the blades were undulating gently, like plants underwater. It gave the disquieting sense that they were waiting.
In the relatively short time since they had rediscovered him, Orsus had grown accustomed to the Orgoth. Their hierarchies were even more rigid than those of his homeland: enforced rapidly and brutally with violence. Any Orgoth leader expected to be obeyed without question or hesitation, and they tended to exude a power and confidence that seemed beyond human—at least partly attributable to the fact that they were something more than mortal, their connection to the Felgoeth infernals meaning that the most powerful among them were reborn to live lifetime after lifetime, each time climbing back from death on a mountain of slain enemies and sacrificed souls.

name: Name
body:
Orsus had first felt this overwhelming power that day on the beach when he had encountered Sabbreth for the first time. He had felt it again each time he had approached one of the Orgoth leaders. And he felt it now, pouring off this new figure in palpable waves that made the hair on his arms stand up.
It is likely that there was a time when Orsus Zoktavir knew fear as a man knows it. He had memories—were they his or someone else’s?—of a child of ten in a basement swarming with rats as cannibalistic monsters butchered his village above. Of coming out to see if his father was still alive, only to instead find himself facing the beast that had slain him.
He had memories of a girl, bright eyed and smiling, her face suddenly streaked with blood. "Why weren’t you there?" she asked. "Why didn’t you protect me?"
But those memories were distant and muffled. It was like he was watching them through a pane of glass. He could see them, but he could not touch them, and they could not touch him. Since the moment the howling axe was fastened to his fist, he had not known the touch of fear. Death was now his constant companion. He no longer walked in its shadow; it was the shadow he cast. And when it closed its hands around his heart at last, he knew that he would welcome it.

name: Name
body: While fear was a stranger, however, disquiet could still reach him, and he felt it in the presence of this new Orgoth. More than the mystical power that poured off her, however. More than the way that she stood in this place not only as if she owned it, but as if she always had, there was one thing that sent a chill deep enough to reach the buried parts of Orsus Zoktavir—the fact that Sabbreth herself stood at this new figure’s side, in a position of uncomfortable deference, a position he had never seen Sabbreth assume and could hardly imagine her in. He stopped before her and inclined his head slightly. He did not kneel. He never had, not for the Orgoth. And while they expected it of all their other soldiers, they never seemed to of him. In a way that not even the empress ever had, the Orgoth seemed to regard him as a peer. "I have heard tales of you, Orsus Zoktavir, betrayed by your empress, by your homeland," the figure said. Sabbreth’s voice was harsh, even when she spoke softly. Not this woman’s. Her voice was like a caress, the slice of a blade across your flesh that seems gentle until you feel the blood come. "You do not disappoint."

name: Name
body:
"I am pleased to hear it," Orsus replied, his eyes sliding to Sabbreth, trying to read her expression, but she wore the helm that she bore into battle, and he could gain nothing from her posture.
"There is no reason you should know me yet," the woman continued, "but you will. I am Hellaine, called the Night Scourge. What we have sent to these shores so far has been only the point of a spear. I represent the rest of the blade. The initial forays are over now. The Reaper Covenant has come."
Orsus had heard the name, though he understood little of the inner workings of Orgoth politics. There were various warlords jostling always for position and power, but they were not the true rulers of the Orgoth, so far as he could tell. That title belonged to the warwitches, the go-betweens for the Orgoth and their Felgoeth masters. No matter which warlord they fought alongside or served, the warwitches had their own hierarchies, bowing ultimately to a Witch Queen and then to the Felgoeth themselves.
The Reaper Covenant was the Witch Queen’s personal army.

name: Name
body:
"I have served," Orsus said simply. "I will serve again."
Hellaine smiled, an expression more horrible on her face than any anger or hatred. "As shall we all, if we are fortunate," she said. "And today you are fortunate indeed, for we have need of you. Far from here and deep in the heart of your former homeland. There is a life there that must be snuffed out."
Orsus squeezed the haft of the fell axe, its voices strangely subdued in the presence of this warwitch.
"That is what I was meant for," was all he said.
***

name: Name
body:
The volozk of Umbrey was the largest in Khador, and they had been within its borders for many days before they got anywhere near the ruins of Old Korska. Yet as they started to draw close, the change in the landscape was unmistakable. Here, the hills rose wilder, the trees grew thicker.
At one time, Umbrey was a true kingdom of its own, not simply a volozk of the Khadoran Empire, and Old Korska had been its capital. That had been centuries ago. Before the first coming of the Orgoth. Before the Motherland as she existed today.
In Sorscha’s time, the ancient capital city had always been a ruin, home to dregg and bogrin and worse things, if the stories were to be believed. She was obviously not the only one who had heard the stories, either, and the closer they got to the ancient city, the more skittish the soldiers became.
The march had not been easy, but it had not been hard. The wind had often whipped at them day and night, driving biting snow into their faces even when none was falling from the leaden grey skies. The weather forced them to skirt around the highest of the Thundercliff Peaks, which added days to their journey.

name: Name
body: More than once, Sorscha had been forced to head off mutterings among the soldiers. Why did they not just head to Skirov and take the rail line south? Why not take an extra day or two and stop at Fort Brunzig to resupply? She had not reached her current position without learning how to stop a mutiny before it began, however. Each time, she identified the source of the complaint, and cut it off sharply, surely, swiftly. When she had still been a girl, she had been helping her father in the garden when she overturned a planter and revealed a venomous snake. Before she could react, her father had driven his shovel down and severed its head in one quick blow. That, she knew, was the way. "We have our orders," was the only explanation she ever vouchsafed to the troops. "Would you like to be the one to gainsay them?" Over the journey, their attitudes toward her had gradually changed. She remembered hazily what it had been like when she was first assigned to this posting. The only thing that prevented the soldiers under her command from treating her with open contempt was her reputation as a genuine hero of the Motherland—and even that wore off in relatively short order, once she showed herself disinclined to command. Instead, they had settled into an easy cohabitation: she content to drink and ignore them, they content to be ignored.

name: Name
body:
Some had bristled early on at this attempt to suddenly reestablish her authority, but they had not bristled for long. Sorscha may have fallen far, but she was used to commanding armies; this tiny serving of outcasts was no match for even this blunted version of her iron will.
Harder to deal with were the cravings. She had been sober since they left the outpost, but every night that grew more difficult. Her skin itched, as though ants were crawling along her arms, and every now and then her fingers literally twitched to reach for a bottle. She slept poorly, and it didn’t help that the kid slept in her tent with her, his presence preventing her from getting up and pacing in the cold air to fight the thirst.
What she fought it with instead was a fantasy. A familiar, hateful face, its mouth filling with blood as she drove the point of Frostfang up under its heavy jaw and through its mad brain.
At first, the kid had tried to keep up with them, and Sorscha had let him. Let him struggle through the snow, which came up nearly to his waist at times. She had told him that who his father was didn’t matter, but it mattered to her. It gave her a cruel pleasure to punish him for being Vlad’s son, for not being hers, though she had never wanted children, not even with Vlad.

name: Name
body: She had expected a pampered and soft prince, and in some ways that was what she got. The kid was inexperienced, clumsy, and at times hopelessly naïve. But he wasn’t as spoiled as she had half-hoped. He tried to march, to work, doing nothing to set himself above the soldiers with whom he toiled, even if they were the lowest that the Winter Korps had to offer. Finally, Sorscha had to admit a grudging respect for the boy. She also had to admit that he was slowing them down, and so she ordered Bear to simply scoop him up in one of its massive armored fists, and he had ridden there for much of the remainder of the journey. When they were a day, maybe two, from the ruined capital, she caught up with the bald-pated Kossite who did much of their scouting. "Anything?" she asked him. He spat in the snow and shook his head, though he was obviously uncomfortable. "Nothing. And yet . . ." "Falko," she said, "if there’s something wrong, I need to know about it." Again, he shook his head. "I have seen nothing. Heard nothing. That itself is wrong. There should be game here, even in this weather. Tracks in the snow. There is nothing. And . . ."

name: Name
body: "And?" "There is nothing, yet I swear we are being watched." Sorscha wanted to tell him not to be an old woman, but she felt it, too. As if the trees themselves had eyes and ears, stooping closer to listen to their conversation. At the same time, she couldn’t afford to acknowledge the fears of her soldiers. That would allow the fear to spread, to amplify. Already, they were spooked enough. Ever since they had made their way into the Kovosk Hills that surrounded Old Korska, the trees had seemed somehow more sinister, skeletal limbs clawing at hats and snatching at coats. And that wasn’t the worst of it. They had maps of the area, albeit hopelessly outdated ones from before Khador had occupied much of Llael. These maps had landmarks that they had been using to navigate, but the landmarks never quite matched up. A creek that curved to the east when it should have gone west. A hill where the charts indicated a depression. "Kommander Kratikoff," Pachek shouted when they were less than two days from Old Korska, "Joseph is gone!"

name: Name
body:
Given the general level of discipline among the ragged group of soldiers under her command, Sorscha’s first assumption was that Joseph had simply stepped aside to piss or pop a squat and hadn’t bothered to inform the soldier nearest him.
"I swear, he was here, and I looked away, and he was gone," Pachek said, obviously close to panic.
Despite the wreck that their boots had churned the snow into, it should have been casually easy to track anyone who broke off. The snow, as Falko had said, was unbroken by tracks other than their own. And yet there was no sign of anyone going off into the woods—or anything coming out of them.
Sorscha called the tracker back, and he examined the trail behind them minutely. "He must have doubled back," the Kossite finally said, though it was clear that he didn’t believe it. "Unless he learned to fly."
Sorscha looked up and scanned the leaden sky above. The storm had stopped, but the clouds remained heavy and dark. There was nothing else to be seen, though. Not even birds. And while the trees gathered close, their bony branches offered little in the way of cover for anything that might have reached down from them and scooped Joseph up.

name: Name
body:
"A deserter," Sorscha said aloud. She didn’t really believe it, any more than Falko did, but it beat admitting to the troops that she had no idea what had become of one of their number. The others murmured at the word, but none were willing to argue.
"Stick close together," Sorscha said, "and watch each other. I don’t want anyone else wandering off."
Yet they did. First Malana. Then Pachek, who Sorscha had moved close to the front of the line when she saw how shaken he was.
"I swear I was watching him," Sergeant Agrinov said. "I kicked a root or something under the snow, and I looked down and he was gone."
Fear was now electric among the remaining soldiers, and Sorscha knew that if she didn’t do something soon, they would all break and scatter, and then, if something was picking them off, they would no longer have any defense against it.
"Listen to me," she said very carefully. "Something is obviously wrong, but it is just an enemy, and an enemy can be beaten. Here’s what we’re going to do . . ."

name: Name
body:
She put Bear at the back, so that he would not muss up the snow in front of them. Then she had all the soldiers form into a single line, shoulder to shoulder, with her and the kid near the center. Their tracks in the snow were clean lines. No possible way for anyone to vanish without leaving a trace. And still, within half an hour, Sergei was gone.
Sorscha thought for a moment that she had lost them. The crackle of panic that shot through the troops was palpable. But she held up her fist and they stopped.
"No one move a damn step," she said. She motioned Falko to her side, and the two of them walked over to where Sergei had been. His tracks made a perfect line in the snow, often smeared by Sergei’s stumbling through drifts, but clear and easily followed until, abruptly, they just . . . stopped.
Falko looked at her with dark, fear-filled eyes, but she was already looking past him. In a tree ahead of them, she saw the bird. It was huge, bigger than any bird she had ever seen. As large as a strong man’s torso, its head and beak stained bright red. It watched her with intelligent eyes.

name: Name
body:
"Kommander . . ." Falko stammered, but he didn’t finish.
In the trees all around them now birds had gathered. She hadn’t seen or heard them come. No one had. They had arrived in breathless silence. Dozens. More than dozens. They were everywhere.
Without a word, Gridya the mechanik turned and ran. Sorscha pulled her gaze from the eerie eyes of the giant crow and saw the snow that Gridya’s footsteps had kicked up drifting slowly back to the ground, but Gridya was already gone.
"Kommander," Sergeant Agrinov said very quietly, "what is . . ."
"Hold," she replied.
One crow flew down from the trees and settled in the snow a half-dozen paces in front of her. Then another. And another. They stood silently on the surface of the snow, occasionally twitching or shaking their feathers. More and more of them descended. As a new one landed, one of the others would take off with a silent beat of its wings, until there was a small cloud of rustling feathers and black, moving bodies ahead of her.
The change came in the blink of an eye. Less than that. The birds were there, flitting about in an unnatural way she had never seen birds behave, and then there was a man in their midst, the birds around him departing, flying back up to perch on their branches.

name: Name
body: The man’s age was impossible to guess. His beard was white as the snow in which he stood, yet he was obviously hale and solid. He was dressed in robes that reminded Sorscha of those she had seen worn by the druids of the Circle Orboros, yet his cloak was not black but a rusty red, decorated with bones and fangs and the black feathers of the birds that still gathered around him. "Greetings, Sorscha Kratikoff," he said, and his voice was the smoothest, most disarming she had ever heard. "I am Bhodan Lesnoi. Zevanna Agha told us of your coming, and we are here to welcome you." END PART 1

name: The Old Ways - Chapter 1 The Old Ways:\nPart 1
